items.prose: Body armor stored in damp underground armories at 85% relative humidity underwent slow hydrolytic chain scission. Tensile testing of individual 1500-denier yarns showed a 62% strength loss; the vest was easily penetrated by a low-velocity .38 Special bullet.

Prolonged surface sentry duty without nylon over-covers exposed outer aramid layers to solar UV-A radiation. The golden fabric turned a dark, brittle brown; surface fibers crumbled into fine yellow dust when rubbed with a thumb.

When tested against a 9mm round, the aged, moisture-degraded aramid panel stopped the slug but the fibers shattered transversely into microscopic needle-like fibrils. The airborne fiber cloud caused severe acute bronchitis in the testing officer.

Brackish marsh water wicked into the unsealed ballistic pack. Repeated drying cycles precipitated sharp halite salt crystals inside the yarn bundles; each footstep ground the internal filaments like abrasive paste, destroying the weave.

Constant skin contact without undergarments saturated the ballistic throat collar with human sweat (pH 4.2). Lactic acid and skin bacteria hydrolyzed the amide cross-bonds, making the flexible neck protector brittle and tearable by hand.

An orderly washed contaminated armor inserts in scavenged dry-cleaning perchloroethylene solvent. The solvent dissolved the thermoplastic polyurethane matrix holding the multi-directional aramid layers, causing total delamination into loose rags.

A cache of twenty ballistic vests buried in clay soil inside a leaking steel drum was excavated after fifteen years. Soil actinomycete bacteria completely consumed the organic polyurethane sizing and cotton stitching, leaving rotting piles of yellow string.

A glancing shrapnel impact on an aged helmet ignited the degraded phenolic binder resin. The localized friction burn melted through four laminations of Kevlar, causing a bubbling blister of toxic aromatic smoke that blinded the wearer.
